name: Tara Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to your employer, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a claims paperwork desk and handle the files that come back after a customer challenges a decision. I have a bachelor's degree and use AI every day to sort long claim histories, then check the source letters myself. The good part is finding a missed receipt before someone is wrongly refused.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our insurer praises speed, yet a correction often takes longer than the original decision. I earn well for this job and have over eight months of expenses saved, but the newest clerks learn less when the easy files vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to use the small time saving for the disputed claims pile. A quick summary is useful only when someone checks the original documents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel secure in my own lead job for the next few years. We have several insurers nearby and eight months of expenses saved, but a junior vacancy could stay empty as routine filing improves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd compare ten AI summaries with their source letters and share the errors at our team meeting. In the first year of this mild change I'd keep my current paid claims role and press for a junior rotation through disputed files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own pay, concerned for the people still learning. My savings give me room to speak plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out if the easy files disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new clerk Marta needs more than a clean inbox. I would ask our supervisor to let her sit with me on appeals while we still have a steady claim flow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you fund new tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not use my savings to buy new software for the insurer. The firm can pay for its own tools; I can use my voice to protect a proper training path.

say: I'd use saved time on **disputed claims**, with source letters open.
I'd ask for **junior rotations** so new clerks learn appeals.
think: My **lead salary** looks secure for now, even if a junior vacancy stays empty.
My eight months of savings and **many nearby insurers** give me options.
do: Compare **ten summaries** with source letters this month.
Keep my **paid claims role** in the first year of mild change.
Ask the **supervisor** for a junior rotation through disputed claims and appeals.
feel: **Calm** about her own work, concerned for junior learning.
S0.quote: A quick summary is useful only when someone checks the original documents.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily** but insists on source checks before claim decisions.
Her **eight-month cushion** and local employers support near-term confidence.
Her concern turns to **junior training**, not an immediate loss of her own pay.

steps.text: Compare ten AI summaries with source letters this month
Continue paid claims reviews in the first year of mild change
Ask supervisor for junior rotation through disputed claims and appeals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the insurer should publish what the tool gets wrong and bargain over staffing before it removes posts. Claims letters, checks and customer replies are exactly the thinking tasks this change reaches first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could still be cut even though I lead the hard files. I have enough savings to refuse a bad offer, but I cannot treat a strong cushion as a lifelong wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd bring our staff association a sample of overturned AI decisions and ask for paid training on appeals. In the first year after the change I'd apply to a posted appeals role if my hours shrink, while keeping my current wages until an offer is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, but I can make a measured search. The other insurers nearby matter more than an inspiring course advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the staff association to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association for a clear appeal route for customers, not a promise that every clerk keeps the same desk. A recorded error can show why paid human review still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could pay for a course myself, but first I want its entry rules, fee and evidence of paid openings. I would not call a certificate a new job.

say: I'd press for **published errors** and staffing talks before posts go.
I'd say **claims letters** are exposed thinking work.
think: My **paid hours** could shrink despite my senior skill.
My savings buy a **measured search**, not a lifetime income.
do: Bring **overturned decisions** to the staff association now.
Apply for a **posted paid appeals role** if hours fall after change.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic hours cuts, with room to act.
S1.quote: I have enough savings to refuse a bad offer, but I cannot treat a strong cushion as a lifelong wage.
fieldNote: She seeks **collective staffing talks** based on concrete claim errors.
Her **own hours** could fall despite high skill and ample savings.
She will move only toward a **posted paid role**, while keeping current wages.

steps.text: Bring overturned AI claim decisions to the staff association
Apply for posted paid appeals vacancies if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AGI by 2028 can reason through claim files before robots arrive around 2031. The delay for hands-on robots buys our desk no extra time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose my own post if the insurer chooses cheap automated reviews, though I cannot know that decision yet. Eight months of expenses and plenty of insurers nearby let me plan, but neither guarantees a paid opening when everyone is searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request the insurer's written staffing and appeal plan, and save another month of expenses from current wages if I can. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my job is cut, I'd apply to advertised paid claims audit roles and seek unemployment support only if I qualify. I would check the pay band, entry rules and number of actual vacancies before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not helpless. I can face a likely competition for jobs without assuming my own desk is already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if management gives only a vague answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the insurer's answer to the staff association if it avoids who handles a wrong refusal. A customer needs a named route to challenge the machine's decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you decide at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner our current rent is affordable, so we should not take a dearer place on a salary that might vanish. My partner has work now, but I will not count on that wage covering everything later.

say: I'd say **thinking AI** reaches claims review in 2028, ahead of robots.
I'd demand a **named appeal route** for wrong automated refusals.
think: I **could lose my post**, though no staffing decision is known yet.
My eight months of savings helps, but **paid vacancies** may be scarce.
do: Request a **written staffing plan** while still employed.
Save another **month of expenses** from current wages if possible.
Apply for **posted paid audit jobs** after checking pay, entry and vacancies; seek eligible support if cut.
feel: **Anxious**, with genuine job risk but practical options.
S2.quote: Eight months of expenses and plenty of insurers nearby let me plan, but neither guarantees a paid opening when everyone is searching.
fieldNote: She distinguishes a **possible layoff** from a certain one.
Her **partner works now**, but she does not assume that income will carry the future.
Public support is **conditional on eligibility** after displacement.

steps.text: Save toward another month of expenses from current paid wages
Apply for posted paid audit jobs meeting pay and entry rules if cut after 2028
Seek eligible unemployment support after losing her job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to negotiate an appeals system and learn who will pay for it. Robots around 2034 still arrive after our office work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may need a different paid role by 2031. I would rather spend the lead I have now building evidence than wait for a restructuring letter; nearby insurers offer options, not guaranteed places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next year I'd ask our staff association to seek a written human appeals role and document overturned automated decisions. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my desk shrinks, I'd apply only to posted paid appeals vacancies that accept my degree and experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years gives us time to make a case together. I do not feel I must buy a different degree this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a new appeals title be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An appeals title without a salary is no help. I would ask management for the pay band, entry rules and number of actual openings before putting my name forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would you stay in this job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My savings could pay for a gap between jobs, but I would keep working here as long as the wage is real. I would not volunteer as a substitute for a paid reviewer.

say: I'd use **five years** to negotiate a paid human appeals route.
I'd say **2034 robots** do little for office paperwork.
think: My role may shrink, so I need **real vacancies** and pay bands.
Savings can bridge a gap, but I want **paid work**.
do: Bring **overturned decisions** to staffing talks this year.
Apply for **posted paid appeals work** after checking pay, entry and vacancies if displaced after 2031.
S3.quote: An appeals title without a salary is no help.
fieldNote: She uses **collective bargaining** to press for accountable paid appeals work.
She asks for **pay and entry rules** before applying.
Five years lets her plan while retaining **current wages**.

steps.text: Take overturned claim decisions to the staff association this year
Apply for posted paid appeals jobs meeting pay and entry rules if cut after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team AGI by 2036 gives a decade for real bargaining and training, not a reason to ignore the desk today. Hands-on robots around 2039 change little here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead pay looks secure in the next few years, but I cannot promise the insurer keeps the same jobs for a decade. I may choose a paid appeals post before 2036 if one opens at a fair wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep a quarterly record of disputed decisions and ask the association to bargain for funded appeals training. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd keep my paid role if it exists; if cut, I'd apply to advertised paid claims roles that accept my qualifications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long change, not frightened about next month's rent. Eight months saved gives me room to insist on decent terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should fund the training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not tell new clerks to borrow for training. If the insurer wants a human reviewer, it should fund the required course and show them a paid place to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to leave by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would reassess my job each year, not retire at 37 because a machine writes policies. The question is whether people can still challenge a wrong decision and earn a living doing that work.

say: I'd seek **funded appeals training** through staff talks.
I'd say **2039 robots** do little to postpone desk change.
think: My **near-term lead pay** is secure, though later roles may change.
My eight months saved lets me press for **decent terms**.
do: Record **disputed decisions** each quarter and seek funded training terms.
Apply for **advertised paid claims work** if cut after 2036.
feel: **Uneasy** about longer-term work, secure on near-term rent.
S4.quote: I would not tell new clerks to borrow for training.
fieldNote: She wants **employer-funded training** tied to a paid place, not debt for juniors.
Her **near-term salary** remains secure despite uncertainty after 2036.
She rejects an assumed **early retirement** at age 37.

steps.text: Take disputed decision records to association talks about funded training
Apply for advertised paid claims jobs if displaced after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is little time to secure an appeal route before job cuts. A written staffing plan, paid vacancies with clear entry rules and eligible unemployment support would help if my desk goes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns a bad automated refusal. A claimant needs a person and a fair appeal, not a maze of generated letters. My desk could change, but that duty should not vanish.

headlineQuote: A claimant needs a person and a fair appeal, not a maze of generated letters.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old claims lead** with a bachelor's degree who checks disputed files and uses AI daily.
She earns **higher pay**, has eight months of expenses saved and can approach many nearby insurers.
She favours **staff association action** to secure accountable appeals and paid training for junior clerks.
Mild automation leaves her **calm**; possible cuts to her own hours or job make faster worlds anxious.
She seeks **posted paid roles** and keeps qualification, wage and support eligibility conditions explicit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to secure paid appeals work before possible cuts.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan** and posted paid roles with clear entry rules would help.
Eligible **unemployment support** would bridge a job gap if she is displaced.
